subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, if 1/(a+c) + 1/(b+c) = 3/(a+b+c), then show that C = 60°.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.77 — SAQ chapter 13 Properties of Triangles, answer 86. Printed appearances: TS 17,19. The only question in the chapter that FINDS an angle rather than proving an identity. Everything is algebra until the very last line, where the cosine rule turns a side relation into an angle. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer. It is not a bare guess: the same book prints 1+1+1+1 for the 4-mark answers 58 and 59 on book p.63 and 1+2+1 for answer 61 on p.64, so both shapes used in this unit are the book's own. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q17 is the Properties of Triangles slot. Together with Q24 (LAQ) this unit holds TWO slots — one of only two units to do so, Matrices being the other. RE-CUT 2026-08-31: this card was filed as SAQ at 4 marks and is now VSAQ at 2. The original label came from the Baby Bullet-Q blueprint for the superseded 75-mark paper; the Sri Chaitanya FAST TRACK IPE Mathematics-IA 2026-27 edition files this chapter as 16 Very Short Answer questions and 11 Short Answer questions, and lists this one among the very short ones (VSAQ 1), not among the short answers. Only the question was taken; the boundary is recorded in docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The mathematics and the steps are unchanged; only the mark scheme moved. The two marks sit on the algebra and the cosine-rule finish; the middle step is kept in full at zero marks. Still unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Clear the fractions
steps.margin_note: Half the marks, and they cover the algebra through to the next step as well. Combine the left side over one denominator, then cross-multiply. Nothing trigonometric happens yet — this is ordinary algebra.

recall.must_convey: That the left side is combined over one denominator, the numerator written as (a+b+c) + c, and the equation cross-multiplied.
accept: combine the fractions and notice the numerator is a plus b plus c plus another c then cross multiply
put over a common denominator and cross multiply
the numerator becomes the perimeter plus c
common denominator teeskoni cross multiply cheyyali

steps.why: Writing b + c + a + c as (a+b+c) + c is the move that makes the cross-multiplication land on a recognisable expansion rather than a mess.
common_mistakes: Adding the fractions by adding numerators and denominators.
steps.memory_tip: Combine the left over one denominator and cross-multiply. Nothing trigonometric happens yet.

steps.label: Expand and simplify
steps.margin_note: No separate mark at this length — it finishes the algebra marked above. Expand both sides fully. Everything cancels except a² + b² − c² = ab — a pure side relation with no fractions left.

recall.must_convey: That both sides expand and cancel down to a² + b² − c² = ab.
accept: expand both sides and everything cancels leaving a squared plus b squared minus c squared equals a b
the algebra reduces to a side relation
it simplifies to a squared plus b squared minus c squared equals ab
expand cheste a square plus b square minus c square equals ab vasthundi
heard_as: a squared plus b squared minus c squared

steps.why: a² + b² − c² is exactly the numerator of the cosine rule for C. Reaching that expression is the signal that the angle is one step away.
steps.memory_tip: Everything cancels except a² + b² − c² = ab — a pure side relation with no fractions.

steps.label: Apply the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Divide both sides by 2ab: the left becomes cos C exactly, and the right becomes 1/2.

recall.must_convey: That dividing by 2ab gives cos C = 1/2, so C = 60°.
accept: divide by two a b so the left is cos C and the right is a half giving C equals sixty degrees
the cosine rule turns it into cos C equals a half
two ab tho divide cheste cos C half, C sixty degrees

steps.why: Dividing by 2ab is chosen precisely because it makes the left side the cosine rule. Any other division would leave something unrecognisable.
common_mistakes: Stopping at a² + b² − c² = ab.
Writing cos C = 1/2 and giving C = 30°.
steps.memory_tip: Divide by 2ab: the left becomes cos C exactly, the right becomes 1/2.
